intro:
These exercises move smart pointers out of the realm of "which type maps to which other language" and into the realm of deliberate ownership design. Each one forces you to read a pointer type as a set of independent statements: how many owners exist, whether they cross a thread boundary, whether the shared value mutates and under which enforcement model, and whether the value's address must stay stable. The composites you build (Rc<RefCell<T>>, Arc<Mutex<T>>, Pin<Box<dyn Future>>) are just those statements layered together.

The lab and the tree-tracing exercises center on the one structural rule that reference counting cannot enforce on its own: owning edges stay strong, observational back-edges become weak. Get that rule right and the cycle problem disappears; get it wrong and you leak. The pinning exercises add the orthogonal concern of address stability, which is a movement question, not an ownership or mutation question.

exerciseSolutions.title: Read each pointer type as an ownership statement
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The point of this exercise is to keep four independent properties separate: owner count, mutation authority, thread sharing, and address stability. A single pointer type usually answers only one or two of these, and the composites answer the rest.

Box<T> provides one owner plus heap indirection. It does NOT provide sharing, reference counting, or interior mutability. Its job is to give a recursive or large type a finite, fixed-size field while keeping single-owner semantics.

Rc<T> provides shared ownership on one thread by incrementing a non-atomic count on clone. It does NOT provide mutation through the shared handle, nor thread safety, because the non-atomic count makes it neither Send nor Sync. Arc<T> provides the same shared ownership but with an atomic count, so it can cross thread boundaries. It does NOT provide arbitrary mutation safety; the atomic count protects only the count, not the data. The single implementation difference between Rc and Arc is atomic versus non-atomic counting, and that difference is exactly what decides single-thread versus cross-thread use.

RefCell<T> provides interior mutability with the borrow rules enforced at runtime: it hands out borrow tokens and panics if you violate the aliasing rule. It does NOT add owners by itself and does NOT provide thread safety. Mutex<T> provides exclusive access only after lock acquisition, moving the aliasing rule's enforcement to lock acquisition rather than the compiler or a runtime panic. It also does NOT add owners by itself; you reach for Arc<Mutex<T>> precisely because Mutex alone gives mutation but not sharing.

Weak<T> is a non-owning edge: it points at an allocation without keeping it alive, so it does not contribute to the strong count. Calling upgrade() returns Option<Rc<T>> (or Option<Arc<T>>), where None means the owner is already gone. Of the listed items, none speak to address stability; that is Pin's exclusive job, which is why the chapter treats it separately.
criteria: Box<T> is stated as one owner plus heap indirection, explicitly without sharing, reference counting, or interior mutability.
Rc<T> and Arc<T> are both shared ownership, differing only in non-atomic versus atomic counting and therefore single-thread versus cross-thread use.
RefCell<T> is named as runtime-checked borrowing that panics on violation, Mutex<T> as exclusive access after lock acquisition; neither is presented as adding owners on its own.
Weak<T> is identified as not keeping the allocation alive with upgrade() returning Option<Rc<T>>/Option<Arc<T>>, and Pin is noted as the only address-stability item (not in this list).

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace the strong and weak edges in the tree sample
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Walk the smart_pointers_tree sample line by line, tracking the counts on each allocation.

After `let leaf = Rc::new(...)`, leaf's allocation has strong count 1 (the `leaf` binding). After `root.children.borrow_mut().push(Rc::clone(&leaf))`, the children vector now holds a second strong handle to the same allocation, so leaf's strong count rises to 2. Rc::clone never copies the node; it increments the non-atomic count and returns another owner of the one allocation. The children edge is therefore a strong, owning edge.

After `*leaf.parent.borrow_mut() = Rc::downgrade(&root)`, root's allocation gains a weak count, not a strong count. Rc::downgrade produces a Weak<Node> that observes root without owning it. So at this point root's strong count is 1 (only the `root` binding) and its weak count is 1 (the leaf's parent edge). The parent edge is an observational, weak edge.

The call `leaf.parent.borrow().upgrade()` must return an Option because a Weak does not keep the allocation alive. Between downgrade and upgrade the strong owners could have been dropped, leaving a dangling intent; upgrade() asks "is the allocation still alive?" and answers Some(Rc) if so or None if not. You cannot dereference a Weak directly precisely because that safety question has not yet been answered; upgrade() is the checkpoint that converts an observation into a temporary strong handle.

The program prints `root strong = 1`. The only strong handle to root is the `root` binding itself. The leaf-to-root edge is deliberately weak, so it contributes nothing to root's strong count. Because the two edges between the nodes are of different kinds (children strong, parent weak), there is exactly one strong cycle's worth of edges missing, and no cycle forms. That is the whole reason the graph stays acyclic and both nodes can eventually drop.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Reference-count trace for each line of the tree sample.
criteria: States that pushing Rc::clone(&leaf) raises leaf's strong count to 2 and that downgrade adds a weak (not strong) count to root.
Explains Rc::strong_count(&root) is 1 because only the leaf-to-root edge is weak and no second strong handle to root exists.
Explains upgrade() returns Option because a Weak does not keep the allocation alive, so the owner may already be gone.
Identifies the children edge as the owning (strong) edge and the parent edge as the observational (weak) edge, which is why no cycle forms.

exerciseSolutions.title: Build a single-thread cache with Rc plus interior mutability
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The instinct under shared ownership is Rc<RefCell<T>>, but RefCell hands out interior borrow tokens and adds a runtime panic mode. For a counter you never need an interior reference; you only ever copy the value out, add one, and write it back. That is exactly the Cell<T> contract, so Cell<u32> is the smaller, sufficient tool and avoids the runtime borrow bookkeeping entirely.

The shared ownership lives in the Rc, not in the Cell. Rc<Stats> lets several handles own one allocation; the Cell<u32> inside that single allocation is what they mutate. record_hit takes &Rc<Stats> (a shared, immutable handle) and still mutates the count, because Cell provides interior mutability: get() copies the current value out, and set() replaces it, neither requiring &mut and neither producing an interior reference. snapshot likewise returns the count by value with get(), never borrowing into the cell.

Cloning the Rc with Rc::clone produces a second owner of the same allocation, so both handles read and write the same Cell. Incrementing through one handle is observed through the other, which is the demonstration that there is one shared allocation, not two copies.

The field-design note: Cell is correct here only because whole-value copy/replace is enough. If a field were larger or needed an interior &mut reference handed out (for example, mutating one element of a Vec in place, or calling a method on the inner value through &mut), Cell would not suffice and you would move that field to RefCell<T>, accepting its borrow tokens and its panic-on-violation runtime check.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Rc<Stats> shares ownership; Cell<u32> supplies copy-out/replace interior mutability without borrow tokens.
criteria: Stats uses Cell<u32> for the count, and record_hit mutates it through &Rc<Stats> with no &mut.
snapshot returns the count by value via get() and never borrows an interior reference.
Two cloned Rc handles read the same updated count, shown by the assert_eq, demonstrating shared ownership of one allocation.
The answer notes Cell is correct because only whole-value copy/replace is needed, and RefCell would be required only if interior references had to be handed out.

exerciseSolutions.title: Poll a hand-written future through Pin
exerciseSolutions.solution:
This mirrors the smart_pointers_pin_poll sample. The poll contract is fixed by the Future trait: `fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Self::Output>`. The receiver is Pin<&mut Self> because the executor must be able to hold an address-sensitive state machine still while it is driven, and the only way to mutate it is through that pinned view.

Inside poll we call self.get_mut() to recover &mut Self. This is permitted because Ticker is a plain struct of Copy fields and therefore implements Unpin automatically. Unpin means "pinning imposes no real constraint on this type because it is freely movable," so Pin::get_mut is sound: there is no address-sensitive invariant to protect. For a !Unpin type (such as a self-referential generated future), get_mut would not be available, and you would need pin-projection or unsafe machinery instead.

The driver builds a no-op Waker via a Wake implementation, wraps it in a Context, and pins the future with Box::pin. Box::pin gives owned, pinned heap storage that can be polled repeatedly; each poll call uses task.as_mut() to produce the temporary Pin<&mut Ticker> the trait demands. We loop, printing each Pending and breaking on Ready.

For remaining = 3: the first poll sees remaining == 3, decrements to 2, returns Pending; the second sees 2, decrements to 1, returns Pending; the third sees 1, decrements to 0, returns Pending; the fourth sees 0 and returns Ready("fired"). That is three Pending results before the single Ready, matching the decrement-then-check structure where zero is only observed on the call after the last decrement.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A hand-written Unpin future driven through Box::pin; three Pending polls precede Ready for remaining = 3.
criteria: poll has the signature taking Pin<&mut Self> and returns Poll::Ready("fired") only when remaining reaches zero.
self.get_mut() reaches the fields, with the note that it is sound because Ticker is movable (Unpin).
The driver pins with Box::pin and polls task.as_mut() in a loop until Poll::Ready.
For remaining = 3 the program reports three Pending polls before the Ready result (asserted).

exerciseSolutions.title: Break a reference cycle and fix a misused pointer
exerciseSolutions.solution:
There are two independent defects: a memory leak from a strong-strong cycle, and a thread-safety mismatch from moving Rc across a thread boundary.

The leak. With `parent: RefCell<Option<Rc<Node>>>` and `children: RefCell<Vec<Rc<Node>>>`, both directions are strong, owning edges. The parent owns the child (in its children vector) and the child owns the parent (in its parent field). Dropping the external `root` and `leaf` bindings lowers each node's strong count, but the mutual edges keep each count at least 1: the parent's allocation is kept alive by the child's parent field, and the child's allocation is kept alive by the parent's children vector. Neither strong count can reach zero, so neither allocation is ever freed. Reference counting cannot collect this on its own.

The fix is the chapter's rule: owning edges stay strong, observational back-edges become weak. Change the parent field to `RefCell<Weak<Node>>`. Set it with Rc::downgrade(&parent), which adds a weak count rather than a strong one, and read it with upgrade(), which returns Option<Rc<Node>> (None once the parent is gone). Now only the children edge is strong; dropping the root lets its strong count reach zero, the allocation frees, and the leaf's weak parent edge cleanly upgrades to None.

The thread-safety mismatch. Rc<Node> uses a non-atomic reference count, so cloning or dropping it from two threads would race on that count. For that reason Rc is neither Send nor Sync, and the compiler rejects moving Rc<Node> across a thread boundary (the closure passed to thread::spawn requires Send). The minimal change for the cross-thread case is to replace Rc with Arc, whose atomic count makes it Send + Sync (when T is). Note that the inner contents must also satisfy the relevant bounds; RefCell is not Sync, so for the cross-thread version the interior-mutability tool must change too.

Finally: switching to Arc alone does NOT make shared mutation safe. Arc solves ownership count, not mutation authority. Two threads sharing Arc<T> can both read, but if they need to mutate, you must add synchronization, typically Arc<Mutex<T>> (shared ownership plus serialized mutation) or redesign toward message passing. Read the composite literally: Arc is the ownership decision, Mutex is the separate mutation decision.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Weak parent edge breaks the leak; Arc plus Mutex is the cross-thread shape (Arc for ownership, Mutex for mutation).
criteria: The leak is attributed to a strong-strong cycle in which neither side reaches a strong count of zero.
The parent field is changed to RefCell<Weak<Node>>, set via Rc::downgrade and read via upgrade() returning an Option.
Rc<Node> is identified as not Send/Sync due to its non-atomic count, with Arc<Node> as the cross-thread replacement.
It is made clear that Arc fixes ownership count only and shared mutation across threads still needs a Mutex (or message passing).

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose pointer types for a mixed-ownership service
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Answer the questions in order for each concern: how many owners, one thread or many, does the shared value mutate, and under which enforcement model. The type then falls out, and each composite reads as a layered statement.

Recursive parser state, single owner. One owner, one thread, no sharing. The only reason a pointer appears at all is recursive shape: a node that contains nodes has no finite size unless the recursive field is behind an indirection. Use Box<T>. It gives one owner plus heap indirection, making the field one pointer wide regardless of depth, with no reference counting or interior mutability implied.

Planning data shared on one thread. Many owners, one thread. If it is read-only after construction, Rc<T> is enough: multiple owners of one allocation, non-atomic count, never crossing threads. If those owners also need to mutate it, the honest type is Rc<RefCell<T>>, read literally as shared ownership plus runtime borrow checking, accepting that borrow violations become runtime panics.

Schema shared read-only across worker threads. Many owners, multiple threads, no mutation. Use Arc<T>. The atomic count makes cloning safe across threads, and because the schema is read-only after construction no further mechanism is needed. The atomic counting is the only cost over Rc.

Retry coordination mutated by several threads. Many owners, multiple threads, mutation required. Use Arc<Mutex<T>>. Read it as two decisions stacked: Arc is shared ownership across threads, Mutex is synchronized mutation where exclusive access is granted only after lock acquisition. Arc alone would give sharing but not safe mutation; the Mutex is the separate enforcement model.

Future stored to be polled later. Use Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ...>>>. A future compiled from async code is a state machine that can hold internal references into its own storage; once polling begins it must not move, or those internal references would dangle. Pin<Box<...>> owns the future on the heap and guarantees its address stays stable across polls. A plain Box<dyn Future> owns it but does not promise address stability, so it cannot satisfy the poll contract for an address-sensitive future.

Operational concerns the Mutex introduces (at least two, and all four matter): lock scope (hold the lock for the shortest critical section so you do not serialize unrelated work); contention (many threads queuing on one lock erodes the parallelism Arc bought you); poisoning (a panic while the lock is held marks it poisoned, so subsequent lock() calls return a PoisonError you must handle); and deadlock risk (acquiring multiple locks in inconsistent order, or re-entering a non-reentrant lock, can hang threads permanently).
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One pointer type per concern, each chosen by owner count, then thread boundary, then mutation model.
criteria: Recursive parser state is Box<T> (one owner, heap indirection for finite size); shared planning data is Rc<T> or Rc<RefCell<T>> on one thread.
The cross-thread read-only schema is Arc<T> and the cross-thread mutable retry state is Arc<Mutex<T>>, each justified by owner count, then thread boundary, then mutation model.
The stored future is Pin<Box<dyn Future>>, justified by the address-sensitive state machine needing to stay put while polled.
At least two operational concerns of the Mutex are named (lock scope, contention, poisoning, deadlock); in fact all four are addressed.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
root children = 1
leaf parent = root
root strong = 1
root weak = 1
leaf parent (after root drop) = none
labSolution.explanation:
The whole lab turns on attach making the two edges between root and leaf deliberately different kinds. `parent.children.borrow_mut().push(Rc::clone(child))` puts a strong, owning handle to the child into the parent's children vector, so the parent owns the child. `*child.parent.borrow_mut() = Rc::downgrade(parent)` stores only a Weak handle in the child's parent field, so the child observes the parent without owning it. RefCell supplies the runtime-checked interior mutability that lets us mutate these fields through the shared Rc handles.

The first two lines print directly from this structure: root has exactly one child, and the leaf's parent edge upgrades successfully (the root is still alive) to yield the name "root". The count lines confirm the shape: `root strong = 1` because the only strong owner of root is the `root` binding itself (the leaf's parent edge is weak and contributes nothing to the strong count), and `root weak = 1` because that single weak parent edge is the one weak reference to root.

The last line is the proof that the graph is acyclic. Inside the println block we `drop(root)`, which removes the last strong owner of the root allocation; its strong count reaches zero and the allocation is freed. The leaf's parent field still holds a Weak, but upgrade() now returns None because the allocation is gone, so parent_name falls through to "none". Had the parent edge been strong, the mutual ownership would have pinned both strong counts above zero and leaked, and this line would still print "root".

reviewAnswers.question: What does Box<T> provide, and which three things that people often associate with smart pointers does it deliberately NOT provide?
reviewAnswers.answer: Box<T> provides single ownership plus heap indirection: one owner of a heap allocation, accessed through a thin pointer-sized handle. It deliberately does NOT provide shared ownership, reference counting, or interior mutability. It is the right tool when you still want one owner but need recursive shape (a finite-sized field for a self-referential type), a smaller stack footprint, or a fixed-size field for a dynamically sized or trait-object value.

reviewAnswers.question: Rc<T> and Arc<T> both give shared ownership; what is the single implementation difference between them, and what consequence does it have for thread boundaries?
reviewAnswers.answer: The single difference is how the reference count is updated: Rc<T> uses a non-atomic count, while Arc<T> uses an atomic count. Because Rc's count can race when touched from two threads, Rc<T> is neither Send nor Sync and cannot cross a thread boundary; Arc's atomic count makes clone and drop safe across threads, so Arc<T> is the cross-thread sibling. Arc pays a small atomic cost for that safety, which is why you use Rc when everything stays on one thread.

reviewAnswers.question: Cell<T> and RefCell<T> are both single-thread interior-mutability tools; when must you choose RefCell<T> instead of Cell<T>, and what failure mode does RefCell add?
reviewAnswers.answer: Choose RefCell<T> when you need to hand out an interior reference to the value, &T or &mut T, rather than only copying, replacing, or swapping whole values, which is all Cell<T> supports. RefCell tracks borrows at runtime and enforces the aliasing rule dynamically, so the failure mode it adds is a runtime panic: borrowing mutably while any other borrow is active (or two mutable borrows) panics instead of being caught at compile time. Cell avoids that panic entirely precisely because it never produces a borrow token.

reviewAnswers.question: Why can reference counting alone never reclaim a cycle, and what edge change turns a cyclic graph back into a collectable acyclic one?
reviewAnswers.answer: Reference counting frees an allocation only when its strong count reaches zero, but in a cycle each node's strong count is kept above zero by the other node's strong edge, so no count ever drops to zero even after all external handles are gone. The repair is to make the back-edge non-owning: keep owning edges strong (Rc/Arc) and change observational back-edges to Weak. A Weak does not contribute to the strong count, so the owning direction can reach zero and free normally, and the weak side simply upgrades to None afterward.

reviewAnswers.question: What invariant does Pin<T> protect, why does Future::poll take Pin<&mut Self>, and why does the distinction not matter for ordinary Unpin types?
reviewAnswers.answer: Pin<T> protects address stability: once a value is pinned it will not be moved, so any address-sensitive invariant (such as internal references into its own storage) stays valid. Future::poll takes Pin<&mut Self> because a future compiled from async code is a self-referential state machine that must not move between polls; the pinned receiver guarantees that while still allowing mutation of the state. The distinction does not matter for ordinary Unpin types, which are freely movable and have no address-sensitive invariant, so pinning imposes no real constraint and methods like Pin::get_mut hand back a plain &mut T soundly.
